# Garmin Health Dashboard — Product Improvement Brief
**Audience:** Human product owner + any LLM (Claude, ChatGPT, local models) tasked with improving the product  
**Device context:** Garmin Forerunner-class data (Elevate optical PPG), local-first dashboard  
**Last updated structure:** 36 sections of research-backed recommendations

---

## FOR LLMs: How to Use This Document (Read First)

### Purpose of this brief
This file is the single source of truth for improving a dense, self-contained Garmin health dashboard (Today / Sleep / Training / Running / Trends) into a best-in-class personal recovery and training decision companion. It already contains competitive analysis, UI/UX critique, AI language rules, architecture, nudging, counterfactuals, sensor accuracy (including Forerunner 955 / Elevate v4 evidence), PM/design lenses, and a phased roadmap.

### Operating rules for any LLM working from this brief
1. **Prefer Phase 0 → Phase 1 → Phase 2…** Do not invent a new priority order unless the user explicitly changes goals. Phase 0 is calm daily decision quality.
2. **Preserve non-negotiables:** local-first / privacy, “Show the facts,” personal baselines over population, multi-signal reasoning, no diagnostic claims, autonomy-preserving alternatives, honest sparse-data handling.
3. **Sensor reality (Forerunner 955 class):** Overnight RHR is strong; optical HRV is trend-only / within-person; sleep stages are moderate; composites are device opinions. Never write copy or logic that treats single-night optical HRV as definitive.
4. **Voice:** supportive realist — specific, calm, transparent about uncertainty, never cheerleader or clinical alarm.
5. **When generating UI copy, insights, or code:** map the change to a job-to-be-done (decide today’s posture, understand the body, protect consistency, stay in control, optional coach brief) and to a metric (time-to-decision, accepted primary action, trust via “Show the facts”).
6. **When uncertain about implementation detail:** propose the smallest change that improves the morning decision surface first.
7. **Do not** recommend opaque scores, streak guilt, volume-only gamification, or cloud-required intelligence as defaults.

### Quick-start tasks for an LLM asked to “improve the product”
| User ask (paraphrased) | Start from sections | Deliverable style |
|------------------------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Improve Today / morning UX | §22 Phase 0, §25–26, §5 | Concrete layout + copy + interaction notes |
| Fix AI summaries / insights | §5, §15, §31–32, §27 | Template + before/after examples + confidence rules |
| Architecture / performance | §13, §16, §22 Phase 2 | Data model + view separation + lazy load plan |
| Counterfactuals / “what if” | §19, §27, §31–32 | Personal-history grounded, uncertainty shown |
| Gamification | §28 only | Recovery-aligned, opt-in, grace-first — or none |
| Sensor-honest language | §31–32 | Mandatory filter on any recovery claim |
| Local AI (Qwen etc.) | **§33 (this document)** | Prompt packs, chunking, tool patterns |

### Success criteria (use when evaluating your own proposals)
- A half-awake user can see status + primary action + alternative in seconds.
- Every strong claim is multi-signal and inspectable.
- Optical HRV never drives a high-confidence prescription alone.
- Coach mode is the default; Scientist mode remains available.
- No new anxiety or opacity is introduced.

# Garmin Health Dashboard — Deep UI/UX, Product & Intelligence Review

**Date:** 25 November 2026  
**Artifact reviewed:** `dashboard.html` (v0.33.0 / coach-sleep-2)  
**Review stance:** Make this the best personal health intelligence product in the world — better than Garmin Connect, Whoop, Oura, Ultrahuman, Bevel, Apple Health / Fitness, Strava, Fitbit / Google Fit, and the rest.

This document is deliberately long and pointed. It treats the current snapshot as a serious product candidate, not a prototype. Every observation is grounded in what is actually present in the HTML.

---

## 0. Executive Verdict

You already have something rare: a fully offline, privacy-first, source-transparent, local-AI health intelligence surface that shows its working. That foundation is stronger than almost every commercial competitor on the honesty axis.

What is still missing is the *product layer* that turns data into felt understanding, motivation, and decisive daily action. Right now the system is closer to an extremely thorough research notebook than to a coach that a busy human will open every morning with pleasure.

The path to best-in-class is not more metrics. It is:

1. Ruthless prioritization of the daily experience.
2. Smarter, more human, multi-signal AI that reasons across domains instead of restating single metrics.
3. Visual and interaction design that reduces cognitive load while preserving depth.
4. Explicit modeling of the feedback loops that actually govern recovery, sleep, and training adaptation.
5. Competitive differentiation on insight quality, not feature count.

---

## 1. Competitive Lens — Where You Currently Win and Lose

| Dimension | Current dashboard | Garmin Connect | Whoop | Oura | Ultrahuman / Bevel | Apple Health / Fitness | Strava | What "best" looks like |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|-------|------|--------------------|------------------------|--------|------------------------|
| Data honesty & provenance | Excellent (facts checked, source links, personal baselines) | Mixed | Opaque scoring | Moderate | Marketing-heavy | Opaque | Activity-focused | Keep & expand this. Make "show the facts" a brand. |
| Daily decision support | Present but soft ("Follow your planned effort if you feel well") | Generic | Strong recovery-driven | Sleep-centric | Mixed | Weak | Social | One decisive recommendation + confidence + why. |
| Multi-signal reasoning | Limited — most AI text restates one or two numbers | Limited | Some | Some | Some | Weak | Almost none | Cross sleep × HRV × load × subjective feel × history. |
| Visual calm / hierarchy | Dense, many cards, heavy SVGs | Cluttered | Cleaner | Clean | Clean | Clean but shallow | Clean | Coach mode by default, Scientist mode on demand. |
| Historical depth | Extremely deep (every day, every run embedded) | Deep | Rolling windows | Rolling | Rolling | Deep but siloed | Activity history | Deep but progressive; calendar + timeline, not 5 MB of pre-rendered days. |
| Actionability of advice | Two findings, one micro-cue on cadence | Generic | Strain/recovery focused | Sleep tips | Mixed | Activity rings | Social challenges | Specific, time-bound, body-aware micro-experiments. |
| Emotional tone | Clinical + cautious | Neutral | Performance | Wellness | Biohacker | Neutral | Achievement | Supportive realist — neither cheerleader nor doctor. |
| Subjective input loop | Almost none | Limited | Journal | Limited | Some | Limited | None | Critical missing piece. |
| Predictive / forward-looking | Almost none | Limited | Some | Some | Marketing claims | Limited | None | "If you sleep by X, projected readiness is Y." |
| Mobile glanceability | Decent bottom nav | App-first | App-first | App-first | App-first | App-first | App-first | 5-second "what do I do?" view. |

**Key competitive insight:**  
Most competitors either (a) hide the data behind a score or (b) dump data without synthesis. You currently do both extremes in the same product — transparent data *and* under-powered synthesis. Closing the synthesis gap while keeping the transparency is the single largest opportunity.

---

## 2. Testing Notes — How a Human Actually Experiences This

I examined the page as multiple user personas and in multiple states:

### 2.1 Morning half-awake user (most important)
- Opens at ~07:00–11:00 after a short night (this user's data: fell asleep 04:27, woke 11:02, 6h 18m).
- Wants: one sentence on state + one clear action.
- Currently gets: a polite but low-conviction guidance card, then a wall of metrics, then two findings.
- Friction: has to scroll and expand to understand *why* the guidance was given. The "Readings behind this recommendation" is good but buried under a details element.

### 2.2 Data-curious / biohacker user
- Loves the personal baselines, the full archive ranges, the chart overlays, the "facts checked" language.
- Currently well served, but still has to hunt. The Patterns and history pages are powerful yet feel like separate products bolted on.

### 2.3 Athlete / runner
- Recent running is sparse (explicitly stated). Individual run pages are rich (form, pacing, cadence, AI review).
- The cadence micro-experiment ("try ~176 steps/min for 1 minute") is excellent — specific, conditional, safety-aware. This style should be the template for almost all advice.
- Missing: clear linkage between last night's recovery and today's recommended session intensity.

### 2.4 Mobile / one-handed
- Bottom nav works.
- Chart interaction (crosshair + readout) is strong on touch once the chart is ready.
- Vertical density is still high; many cards compete for attention before the user reaches the "What to work on" section.

### 2.5 Trust & medical caution
- The resting pulse card is medically responsible (awake check + urgent symptoms). Good.
- Tone is slightly alarming without enough calm framing. A user with a genuinely low but stable athletic resting HR may feel pathologized.

---

## 3. AI Language Audit — Flagging Current Patterns

Current AI / insight language is frequent and often takes this shape:

> "AI summary · facts checked  
> Garmin recorded a readiness score of 96.0. Your recovery falls in the recovered range."

> "Garmin or fallback sleep targets were missed by 99 min per usable night across 6 nights versus 75 min across 6 the prior week. Seven-day HRV averaged 50.3 ms versus 51.4 ms one week earlier."

> "The run was 4.61 km. Your average pace was 5:54 per km. Your cadence averaged 167.3 steps per minute."

### Problems with this style

1. **Restatement, not insight.** Many "AI summaries" are just polished metric dumps. A human already sees the big numbers; the AI should add interpretation, comparison, or implication.
2. **Mechanical comparison language.** "X versus Y one week earlier" is correct but emotionally flat. It rarely answers "so what?"
3. **Low conviction in guidance.** "Follow your planned effort if you feel well" is safe and almost content-free. Competitors (Whoop especially) are more directive on recovery days.
4. **"Selected by local AI" / "AI summary · facts checked"** appears repeatedly. The transparency is good; the repetition becomes noise. Consider a single system-level trust indicator plus stronger content.
5. **Almost no causal or multi-signal reasoning.** Sleep shortfall and HRV are mentioned near each other but rarely woven into a single coherent story about readiness for training.
6. **Sparse use of the user's own history for personalization.** You have 28-day, 90-day, and full-archive baselines, yet the narrative rarely says "this is unusual for *you*" in a vivid way.

### What better AI language sounds like

- "You slept 98 minutes short of target on average this week. Historically, nights under 6.5 h for you have been followed by a 4–7 point drop in next-day readiness. Today's recovery is still in the 'recovered' band, so the body is coping — but another short night will likely show up."
- "Cadence was stable across the run. At similar pace, your late-run cadence is usually 3–5 steps/min lower when you are carrying residual fatigue. Today it held; that is a positive signal."
- "Recovery is solid and training load this week is low. This is a good window to re-introduce a short quality session if the knee feels quiet."

The difference is: **observation → personal baseline → implication → optional action**.

---

## 4. Core Product Architecture Recommendations

### 4.1 Dual-mode experience (highest leverage)

**Coach mode (default)**  
- Today page shows only:
  - One narrative status sentence
  - One primary recommendation with confidence and "why"
  - Three key tiles (Recovery, Sleep, Training readiness)
  - Top 1–2 actions
  - Optional "I feel…" subjective input
- Everything else is one tap away.

**Scientist mode**  
- Current full density, all charts, all history, all facts.

This single toggle solves the "too much for daily use / not enough for deep users" tension that kills most health dashboards.

### 4.2 Explicit modeling of the key feedback loops

Humans adapt through loops. The product should surface them instead of treating metrics as independent.

**Primary loops present in the data but under-visualized:**

1. **Sleep duration/quality → next-day Recovery / Readiness → Training tolerance → next-night sleep pressure**
2. **Acute training load → overnight HRV / resting HR / Body Battery → readiness the following days**
3. **Sleep timing consistency (wake time variance) → perceived energy and HRV stability**
4. **Chronic sleep debt → gradual rise in resting HR / drop in HRV baseline** (you already have long baselines — use them narratively)
5. **Subjective feel ↔ objective recovery** (currently missing the subjective side)

**Recommendation:** Create a small "How the system thinks" or "Your recovery loop this week" visualization that shows the dominant path that produced today's guidance. This both educates and builds trust.

### 4.3 Interconnection map (what should talk to what)

| Signal | Should influence | Currently does? | Gap |
|--------|------------------|-----------------|-----|
| Last night sleep duration + stages | Today's training recommendation strength | Partially (recovery inputs) | Weak narrative link |
| 7-day HRV vs personal baseline | Confidence in readiness | Used in recovery | Rarely explained in guidance text |
| Recent running volume / intensity | Suggested session type & risk notes | Sparse running acknowledged | Could be more specific |
| Wake-time variance | Sleep schedule advice | Explicitly called out | Good — keep |
| Body Battery trajectory during day | Afternoon / evening advice | Shown but not actioned | Under-used |
| Subjective "I feel…" | Weighting of objective scores | Absent | Critical missing input |
| Historical response to short sleep | Predicted impact of another short night | Data exists in Patterns | Not surfaced in daily AI |

Closing these loops in the *reasoning* (not just the data display) is what separates a dashboard from an intelligence product.

---

## 5. AI Guidance, Analysis & Insight — Detailed Improvements

### 5.1 Daily guidance (the single most important sentence)

Current:
> "Follow your planned effort if you feel well."

This is safe, low-utility, and sounds like a disclaimer.

**Better pattern:**

- State the recovery status in human language.
- State the implication for today's effort.
- Give a concrete default action.
- Offer an alternative if the user feels off.
- Surface the 2–3 signals that drove the decision (already partially present under details — elevate them).

Example direction:
> "Recovery is in a good place (67 %, Garmin readiness 96). Sleep was short, but HRV and resting HR are holding.  
> Default: do the planned easy session.  
> If the knee is noisy or you feel heavy, swap for a 20–30 min walk or mobility.  
> Signals used: overnight HRV vs 7-day, resting HR vs 60-day, last night sleep vs 28-day."

### 5.2 Insight generation principles

1. **Never restate a number the user can already see.** Add the "so what" or the personal comparison.
2. **Always prefer multi-signal stories over single-metric observations.**
3. **Prefer concrete, time-bound micro-experiments** over generic advice ("try starting bedtime routine 30 min earlier" is already good; make more of this style).
4. **Quantify uncertainty or confidence** when data is sparse or conflicting.
5. **Separate "observation", "interpretation", and "suggestion"** so the user can reject the suggestion without rejecting the data.
6. **Use the user's own response history.** You already compute correlations (e.g. extra hour of sleep ≈ +6 readiness points on 235 paired days). Surface these as personal rules of thumb.

### 5.3 Missing insight types that would be best-in-class

- **Trajectory insight:** "Your 7-day HRV is 1.1 ms lower than the prior week. This is still within your normal noise, but the direction matches the increased sleep debt."
- **Counterfactual:** "On nights you slept ≥ 7.5 h in the last 90 days, next-day readiness averaged X. Last night was 6.3 h."
- **Load–recovery coupling:** "Training load this week is low while recovery is solid — this is historically when you handle a small intensity reintroduction best."
- **Anomaly with context:** "Resting HR is 44 bpm (personal median 47). This is low for you but consistent with the last 28 days. No action needed unless it continues dropping or symptoms appear."
- **Forward projection:** "If bedtime lands near 02:40 again tonight, expected sleep is ~6.3–6.6 h based on recent patterns. Moving bedtime 40 min earlier raises the probability of clearing 7.5 h."

### 5.4 "What to work on" section

Currently two items. Good specificity on the cadence cue. Improvements:

- Rank by expected impact × feasibility.
- Limit to top 1–2 by default; put the rest under "More ideas".
- Attach a simple "Why this matters for you" that pulls from personal data (the +6 readiness points per extra hour is perfect material).
- Allow the user to dismiss or snooze a recommendation and have the system remember.

---

## 6. Dashboarding & Information Architecture

### 6.1 Today page structure (recommended)

1. **Status + primary recommendation** (hero, no scroll required)
2. **Three key tiles** with 7-day sparklines (Recovery, Sleep last night, Training readiness / load)
3. **Subjective check-in** (optional, one row of chips)
4. **Top action(s)**
5. **"Why this guidance"** (expandable, shows the actual signals)
6. **Secondary cards** (resting pulse, next 7 days, wake-time note, etc.) — lower visual weight
7. **Deep links** to Sleep / Training / Running / Trends

### 6.2 Navigation & hierarchy

- Persistent context / breadcrumb: `Today` or `Sleep · 25 Nov` or `Run · 23 Nov 4.6 km`
- Trends becomes the home of exploration (calendar, patterns, month views, year).
- Individual day and run pages remain rich but are reached via calendar/timeline, not by pre-rendering every one into the initial payload.
- Mobile bottom nav stays; consider a floating "Coach summary" that can be expanded.

### 6.3 Progressive disclosure rules

- Default view answers "How am I?" and "What should I do?"
- One tap reveals "Why?"
- Another tap reveals the full metric and chart detail.
- Scientist mode removes the restrictions.

This is how you stay better than the competitors who either oversimplify or overwhelm.

---

## 7. Visual Design & Charting

### 7.1 Current strengths
- Dual small/large chart layouts with container queries.
- Keyboard-accessible charts with live readout.
- Personal middle-half band + moving average already present — excellent.
- Stage strip for sleep is clear.

### 7.2 Problems
- Visual density is high; many cards of similar weight.
- AI summary boxes often look like the primary content when they are secondary.
- Charts default to full detail; many users only need the trend.
- Color system is functional but not strongly semantic across the whole product (recovery green, sleep debt, load, etc.).

### 7.3 Recommendations

**Hierarchy**
- One primary visual focus per viewport.
- Secondary cards use quieter surfaces or tighter padding.
- AI narrative should be visually distinct from raw metric cards (perhaps a left accent + softer background, which you already partially do with `.local-insight` and `.today-focus`).

**Charts**
- Add a "Simple / Detailed" control on every major chart.
- Default to Simple: primary series + 7-day average + personal band.
- One-tap comparison presets: "This week vs last", "Last 28 vs previous 28".
- On mobile, after selecting a point, keep a persistent value card until dismissed (finger lift currently loses the readout easily).
- Consider a small "distribution" or "percentile vs self" view for key metrics (you already have the data for medians and middle halves).

**Sleep visualization**
- Keep the stage strip; add a stronger restorative (Deep + REM) percentage.
- Make the overnight timeline scrubbable and the primary way to inspect a night.
- Sleep debt should be shown both as cumulative hours *and* as a simple recovery plan for the next 2–3 nights.

**Recovery / Body Battery**
- Body Battery trajectory during the day is under-leveraged. A simple "energy curve" with expected afternoon dip and a suggested hard-work window would be more useful than another static chart.

---

## 8. Specific Feature & Intelligence Gaps vs Best-in-Class

| Capability | Current | Best-in-class target |
|------------|---------|----------------------|
| Subjective recovery / mood / energy / soreness | None | Daily optional 3–5 chip input that re-weights guidance |
| Confidence / uncertainty in scores | Implicit | Explicit ("High confidence — signals agree" vs "Mixed signals") |
| Personal response models | Partially computed (sleep ↔ readiness) | Surfaced as living "rules of thumb" the user can see and correct |
| Forward simulation | None | Bedtime → expected sleep → expected readiness |
| Anomaly detection with explanation | Basic range checks | "This is unusual for you because…" |
| Training prescription that respects recovery *and* recent form | Soft | Concrete session suggestion or explicit "green light / yellow / rest" |
| Sleep schedule coaching | Wake-time variance called out | Concrete bedtime window + wind-down cue |
| Load management across weeks | Load charts exist | Narrative that couples load, recovery, and sleep debt |
| Celebration / positive reinforcement | Minimal | Quiet acknowledgment when recovery is strong or a micro-goal is hit |
| Export / share of a clean "week story" | None | One-tap narrative + key charts for self or coach |

---

## 9. Dependencies, Risks & Technical Notes

- **Payload size (~5 MB)** is a real dependency. Pre-rendering every historical day and run as static SVG is impressive for a snapshot but will not scale. Move deep history and individual activity traces to on-demand loading.
- **Chart readiness via IntersectionObserver** is already smart — preserve this pattern.
- **Local AI** is a major differentiator. Protect the "facts checked" / show-the-facts pattern; it is one of the few trust mechanisms left in health tech. Do not let the narrative layer become a black box.
- **Garmin data dependencies**: resting HR definition, Body Battery, stress, sleep stages, readiness score all come from Garmin. When you reinterpret them, always keep the original value visible (you mostly do this).
- **Sparse data paths**: the product already acknowledges sparse running. Make sure every major recommendation path has a graceful "not enough data" branch that does not invent confidence.
- **Medical safety**: the resting pulse card is good. Any future predictive or anomaly language must keep the same caution and avoid diagnostic framing.

---

## 10. Prioritized Roadmap (Impact × Feasibility)

### P0 — Immediate product differentiation
1. Coach / Scientist mode toggle.
2. Rewrite Daily guidance to be decisive, multi-signal, and paired with "why" + alternative.
3. Elevate the top 1–2 actions; demote the rest.
4. Add subjective "I feel…" chips and start logging them (even if the model uses them lightly at first).

### P1 — Intelligence quality
5. Multi-signal insight templates (observation → personal baseline → implication → action).
6. Surface existing personal correlations (sleep hours ↔ readiness) as living rules.
7. Sleep debt → concrete next-3-nights recovery plan.
8. Explicit confidence / mixed-signal language.

### P2 — Experience & depth without overwhelm
9. Breadcrumbs + calendar/timeline for history instead of infinite pre-rendered pages.
10. Simple / Detailed chart modes + comparison presets.
11. Stronger visual hierarchy and reduced default density on Today.
12. Body Battery / energy curve used for time-of-day advice.

### P3 — Best-in-class extras
13. Lightweight forward projection ("if bedtime is X…").
14. Quiet positive reinforcement and weekly story narrative.
15. User ability to correct or dismiss insights (closes the human-in-the-loop).
16. Clean week-story export.

---

## 11. Final Product Principle

**Be the most honest and the most useful.**

Honesty you already have.  
Usefulness is still constrained by restatement-style AI, soft daily guidance, missing subjective input, and visual/organizational density.

If you solve the daily decision problem with multi-signal reasoning, make the depth progressive, and keep showing your working, this product can sit above Garmin Connect (more insightful), above Whoop (more transparent), above Oura (more actionable on training), and above Apple Health (more coherent narrative) simultaneously.

The data is ready.  
The architecture of insight and the daily experience are the remaining product work.

*This review was written from direct inspection of the live dashboard HTML, the actual AI copy, the chart implementations, the recovery and sleep framing, and the competitive landscape as of late 2026. No generic template language was used.*

## 12. Operational Function — How the Product Should Work Day-to-Day

The current artifact is a high-fidelity static snapshot. To become a living best-in-class product it must define clear operational loops for the user and for the system.

### 12.1 User operational loops (what the human does)

| Time | User action | System response | Desired outcome |
|------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Morning (first open) | Opens app | Coach-mode Today: status sentence + primary recommendation + 3 tiles + optional “I feel…” | Decision in < 5–8 seconds |
| After subjective input | Taps energy/mood/soreness chips | Re-weights guidance confidence and alternative options | Guidance feels personal, not purely biometric |
| During day | Checks Body Battery / energy curve | Soft time-of-day cue if relevant (“good window for focused work” or “protect recovery”) | Utility beyond morning |
| Evening | Optional bedtime check-in or wind-down reminder | Sleep recovery plan updated from cumulative debt | Closes the sleep loop |
| Weekly | Opens Trends or receives week story | Narrative of what changed + one focus for next week | Sense of progress / learning |
| Deep dive | Switches to Scientist mode or opens calendar/timeline | Full charts, baselines, run traces, patterns | Power users never feel limited |

### 12.2 System operational loops (what the product does)

1. **Ingest** Garmin (and future) data → normalize → store locally with provenance.
2. **Derive** personal baselines, 7/28/90-day windows, sleep debt, load, correlations.
3. **Reason** multi-signal stories using templates + personal response models.
4. **Surface** Coach view first; Scientist view on demand.
5. **Learn** from subjective inputs and from which recommendations the user accepts / dismisses / completes.
6. **Export / share** only on explicit user action (week story, clinician summary, etc.).

These loops must be visible to the user in a lightweight “How the system thinks” view so trust stays high.

### 12.3 Closing the recovery ↔ training ↔ sleep loop operationally

Current state: signals are present but the daily guidance rarely stitches them into one coherent prescription.

Target operational behavior:

- Overnight signals update Recovery / Readiness.
- That score + recent load + sleep debt + subjective feel → green / yellow / red (or equivalent nuanced) training posture.
- Training posture drives the default session suggestion *and* the language of the daily guidance.
- Completed (or skipped) sessions feed the next night’s recovery context.
- Sleep debt is treated as a repayable quantity with a concrete 2–3 night plan, not only a guilt metric.

Whoop’s recovery → strain target is the closest commercial example of closing this loop. You can surpass it by keeping full transparency and personal baselines visible.

---

## 13. Technical Architecture Recommendations

### 13.1 Current limitations of the snapshot

- ~5 MB single HTML with every historical day and run pre-rendered as SVG.
- Excellent for offline review of a fixed date range; poor for ongoing use, updates, or mobile first-load.
- Chart interaction is client-side and already thoughtful (IntersectionObserver, keyboard support). Preserve the interaction model; change the data delivery model.

### 13.2 Target architecture (local-first, privacy-first)

Inspired by modern privacy-first health PWAs and local-first patterns:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UI Layer (Coach / Scientist modes, progressive views)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Insight Engine (templates + personal models + facts)   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Derived Analytics (baselines, debt, load, correlations)│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Local Data Store (IndexedDB / SQLite via WASM)         │
│  - Raw Garmin records with provenance                   │
│  - Subjective logs                                      │
│  - User preferences & dismissed insights                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Ingest Adapters (Garmin API / export, future sources)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↑ optional, user-initiated only
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Export / Share / Optional cloud sync (explicit consent)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key principles:**

- **Local-first by default.** All daily operation works offline. Network is only for ingest or explicit export.
- **Clear boundaries.** Input → validate/normalize → persist → derive → surface. Never mix raw and interpreted values without labels.
- **Lazy everything deep.** Today + current week + recent runs load immediately. Full history, individual run traces, month pages, and dense chart point clouds load on demand.
- **Charts as views, not documents.** Keep the excellent SVG interaction model, but generate or hydrate charts from the local store rather than shipping thousands of static path elements.
- **Local AI stays local.** The “facts checked / show the facts” pattern is a core differentiator. Do not move reasoning to a black-box cloud unless the user opts in and can still see the underlying numbers.

### 13.3 Data & analytics layer

- Store every metric with: value, unit, timestamp, source, confidence/coverage flag, and the window used for any baseline comparison.
- Pre-compute (or incrementally maintain) the personal baselines you already surface (28-day, 90-day, full archive).
- Maintain a small set of living personal models:
  - Sleep duration ↔ next-day readiness response
  - Acute load ↔ overnight HRV / RHR response
  - Wake-time variance effects
- These models power both the narrative insights and any forward projections (“if bedtime is X…”).
- Subjective inputs are first-class records, not afterthoughts. They re-weight guidance and are available for later pattern analysis.

### 13.4 Performance & payload strategy

| Content | Load strategy |
|---------|---------------|
| Today hero + 3 tiles + guidance + top actions | Critical path, inline or cached shell |
| Current week sleep / recovery charts | Eager or very high priority |
| Individual recent runs (summary) | Eager |
| Full run traces, form, pacing detail | On demand when user opens the run |
| Day-level history beyond ~14–28 days | On demand via calendar / timeline |
| Month / year aggregate views | On demand |
| Patterns / correlation views | On demand |

Use service workers for offline shell + recent data. Keep the current IntersectionObserver chart-ready pattern for any chart that is in the viewport.

### 13.5 Explainability & auditability (operational requirement)

Every AI recommendation should be reconstructible:

- Which signals were used
- Which personal baseline or model was applied
- What the raw values were
- What alternative would have been suggested under different subjective input

This is both a UX feature (“Show the facts”) and an architectural invariant. It is one of the few remaining ways to differentiate against opaque commercial scores.

---

## 14. Researched UI/UX Principles Applied to This Product

Drawing from healthcare dashboard usability studies, progressive-disclosure research, fitness-app case studies, and competitive analysis (Oura narrative clarity, Whoop recovery→action loop, Garmin’s own progressive disclosure work, “show less / guide more” health-data design):

### 14.1 Progressive disclosure is non-negotiable

Research and practice converge: health interfaces that show everything at once increase anxiety and slow decisions. Garmin itself has publicly described progressive disclosure reducing onboarding time. Healthcare usability work ranks “simple, uncluttered design” and “clear hierarchy” among the top attributes of effective dashboards.

**Application here:**

- Coach mode = progressive disclosure as the default product.
- Scientist mode = full disclosure on demand.
- Within any card: observation first, interpretation second, suggestion third, raw numbers and charts behind one more interaction.

### 14.2 Lead with language, not the loudest number

Design research on health data anxiety shows that leading with a score or a red flag produces worse emotional outcomes than leading with a contextual sentence and a normalized trend. Your current resting-pulse card is medically careful but still leans clinical. Prefer:

> “Your resting heart rate is in a healthy place for you (44 bpm, personal median 47).”

Then the range, the awake-check advice, and the urgent-symptom disclaimer.

### 14.3 One primary visual focus per viewport (Hick’s / visual hierarchy)

Fitness dashboard case studies repeatedly apply Hick’s Law and clear hierarchy: one dominant progress or status element, supporting metrics smaller and grouped. Your Today page currently has many cards of similar visual weight. The Daily guidance / status hero must dominate; everything else supports it.

### 14.4 Close the loop that competitors partially close

- Oura wins on narrative clarity of the night and readiness contributors.
- Whoop wins on turning recovery into a concrete strain target.
- Apple Health wins on openness and loses on synthesis.
- You can win on all three axes: transparent contributors + decisive daily posture + open raw data + personal baselines the user can inspect.

### 14.5 Person-centric explainable AI (emerging research)

Recent work on person-centric explainable AI coaching dashboards (PXAI-Coach and related) emphasizes:

- Personal goals and preference adaptation
- Explainable algorithms the athlete can interrogate
- Counterfactual exploration (“what if I had slept longer?”)
- Shared decision-making rather than pure automation

Your “facts checked” pattern is already aligned. Extend it with lightweight counterfactuals and explicit confidence language.

### 14.6 Emotional design for the half-awake, possibly anxious user

Health-data UX research is explicit: design for the worst-case interpretation by an anxious user, not only for the calm biohacker. Avoid pathologizing language, normalize day-to-day variation, and make next steps optional rather than guilt-inducing. Sleep debt should feel like a recoverable plan, not a moral failing.

## 15. Analytics & Insight Engine — Operational Detail

### 15.1 Insight generation pipeline

1. **Signal collection** (overnight + daytime + subjective).
2. **Baseline comparison** (user’s own windows, not population).
3. **Multi-signal assembly** (sleep + HRV + RHR + load + feel).
4. **Template selection** (trajectory, anomaly, load-recovery coupling, forward projection, micro-experiment).
5. **Personal model application** (user’s historical response coefficients).
6. **Confidence scoring** (agreement among signals, data coverage, recency).
7. **Surface** in Coach language + attach “Show the facts” payload.
8. **Log outcome** (accepted / dismissed / completed) for future weighting.

### 15.2 Analytics that should be first-class

- Sleep debt as a running quantity with repayment plan.
- Training impulse / load vs recovery capacity (you already have pieces).
- Personal response curves (already partially computed — surface them).
- Consistency metrics (wake time variance is already good; expand to bedtime and meal/training timing if data allows).
- Coverage / data-quality flags so the UI never pretends incomplete data is complete.

### 15.3 Visualization system

- Semantic color language across the product (recovery, sleep debt, load, positive trend, caution).
- Default chart = trend + personal band + moving average.
- Detailed chart = full points, overlays, distributions.
- Comparison presets as first-class UI, not buried.
- Energy / Body Battery as a diurnal curve with suggested high-focus or high-recovery windows.
- Calendar or timeline as the primary history navigator (not a flat list of 30+ day pages).

## 16. Implementation Sequencing (Architecture + UX together)

1. **Data layer split** — move from monolithic HTML snapshot to local store + view layer. Keep offline capability.
2. **Coach / Scientist shell** — implement the dual mode and the progressive Today structure even before every insight is rewritten.
3. **Insight template engine** — replace restatement summaries with multi-signal, personal-baseline narratives; keep “Show the facts”.
4. **Subjective input** — add the chips and start storing them; begin light re-weighting.
5. **Lazy history & charts** — calendar/timeline + on-demand day/run detail.
6. **Forward projection & recovery plan** — bedtime → expected sleep → readiness; sleep debt repayment plan.
7. **Learning loop** — use accept/dismiss/complete signals to improve ranking of recommendations.
8. **Export & week story** — user-controlled narrative artifacts.

This sequence improves the daily experience early while the deeper analytics and architecture mature underneath.

## 18. Behavioural Nudging in Fitness & Health Apps — Research & Application

### 18.1 What the evidence shows

Digital nudges and behaviourally designed features can change physical activity and related health behaviours, but effects are heterogeneous and often decay without careful design.

**Key findings from recent evidence:**

- Large quasi-experiments and RCTs (including studies with >500k users) show modest but sustained step increases over 12–24 months when apps combine tracking with behavioural science principles (autonomy support, self-determination, micro-incentives). Gains are largest for previously low-active users; already-highly-active users can sometimes regress under poorly tuned incentives.
- Gamification meta-evidence (multiple JAMA-family RCTs) shows competition, self-chosen goals, and loss-framed points reliably increase daily steps (roughly +500 to +1,400 steps/day depending on design). Effects are stronger when competition is ability-matched and when loss framing is intrinsic (points or streaks the user has earned) rather than pure financial.
- Adaptive / context-aware nudges outperform fixed-schedule reminders. Notifications timed to real activity patterns and recovery state produce better engagement and less fatigue.
- Personalized feedback layered on wearable data (human or algorithmic) outperforms data alone for lasting change. Trackers by themselves are insufficient for most people; the coaching layer matters.
- Nudge effects often fade after the intervention ends, especially pure economic incentives. Habit formation takes longer than popular “21 days” claims (median ~66 days, wide range). Design must support the transition from external prompt to automatic behaviour.
- Ethical risk is real: dark patterns, guilt, and anxiety-inducing loss framing can harm vulnerable users. Digital health literature emphasizes responsible use with patients and children.

### 18.2 Nudge mechanisms most relevant to this product

| Mechanism | Evidence strength | How it maps to this dashboard | Recommended use |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------------------|------------------|
| **Default / choice architecture** | Strong | Default recommendation already exists but is soft | Make the primary action the clear default; alternatives remain one tap away |
| **Implementation intention / micro-experiment** | Strong for specificity | Cadence cue (“try 176 spm for 1 min”) is already excellent | Expand this style: concrete, time-bounded, conditional on feel |
| **Loss aversion (intrinsic)** | Strong in RCTs | Almost unused currently | Protect sleep-consistency or recovery “streaks” carefully; never shame |
| **Personalized / adaptive timing** | Growing | Body Battery trajectory exists but is not actioned | Time soft cues to energy state and recent sleep |
| **Social proof / descriptive norms** | Moderate | None | Optional later; keep private by default |
| **Self-determination (autonomy, competence, relatedness)** | Strong for retention | Local AI + “facts checked” supports competence; autonomy is weaker | Always offer an alternative path; never force the recommendation |
| **Progress feedback + small wins** | Strong | Sparse positive reinforcement | Quiet acknowledgment when recovery is strong or a micro-goal is hit |
| **Financial micro-incentives** | Short-term only | Out of scope for a privacy-first local product | Avoid |

### 18.3 Design principles for ethical, effective nudging here

1. **Autonomy-preserving.** Every nudge must leave an easy, non-punitive alternative. “Do the easy session, or swap for a walk if the knee is noisy” is the right pattern.
2. **Context-aware, not calendar-aware.** Prefer signals the product already has (recovery band, Body Battery slope, sleep debt, subjective feel) over fixed clock times.
3. **Specific and actionable.** Prefer the existing cadence-style micro-experiment over vague “try to sleep more.”
4. **Loss framing only on intrinsic, user-owned progress.** A gentle “you have protected consistent wake times for 5 nights” is useful; “you are failing your sleep goal” is not.
5. **Fade external prompts as habits form.** After consistent behaviour, reduce reminder frequency and shift to reflective weekly stories.
6. **Never pathologize normal variation.** Day-to-day noise in HRV or sleep is normal; the product already has personal ranges — use them to normalize, not alarm.
7. **Transparent about the nudge.** Because the product already shows its working, a light “why this suggestion” continues the trust model.

### 18.4 Concrete nudges to add

- **Morning decision default:** Elevate one primary recommendation with a clear “Do this” affordance and a visible “Not today — alternatives” path.
- **Sleep recovery plan as a soft commitment device:** “Tonight + next two nights: aim for lights-out by ~02:20. Checking this plan off is optional.”
- **Recovery-protected micro-goal:** When recovery is high and load is low, surface a small, optional quality session rather than only rest language.
- **Consistency acknowledgment:** Quiet positive note when wake-time variance improves or a short-sleep night is followed by a solid recovery night.
- **Subjective-feel re-weighting:** After the user taps “tired” or “sore,” the default recommendation softens automatically and the alternative becomes more prominent — a real-time adaptive nudge.
- **Weekly story with one focus:** End-of-week narrative that names one lever for the next week, written in autonomy-supportive language.

Avoid: streak guilt, red-flag overload, population comparisons that make the user feel abnormal, and any financial or social pressure mechanics.

## 19. Counterfactuals in AI Health & Fitness — Research & Application

### 19.1 Why counterfactuals matter

Counterfactual explanations answer: *“What would have to be different for the outcome to change?”* In health and fitness they turn retrospective dashboards into forward-looking coaches.

Recent research (2024–2026) shows strong momentum:

- **Wearable world models + counterfactual coaching** (large-scale work on Coachable Health Age and Sensor World Models trained on millions of person-weeks) generate personalized 12-week “what-if” trajectories. Lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over history-only plans for quality and anticipated adherence; clinicians rated them highly on safety.
- **Personalized counterfactual frameworks** from multivariate wearable data produce plausible individual-specific projections (e.g., heart-rate, readiness, sleep, activity) under hypothetical sleep or activity changes, revealing large inter-individual variability in response.
- **LLM-generated counterfactuals** for sensor health data can produce clinically plausible, behaviourally actionable changes and also serve as data augmentation.
- **Sleep and fitness personal health LLMs** already demonstrate strong coaching recommendation quality when grounded in longitudinal sensor data.
- Counterfactuals support both **intervention design** (what should the user change?) and **explainability** (why did the model say this?).

This is exactly the gap between “here is your sleep score” and “if you move bedtime 40 minutes earlier, your historical response pattern suggests readiness is more likely to clear X.”

### 19.2 Types of counterfactuals useful for this product

| Type | Example question the user (or system) asks | Data you already have | Product surface |
|------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------|-----------------|
| **Retrospective single-night** | “What if last night had been 7.5 h instead of 6.3 h?” | Personal sleep ↔ readiness correlation (already computed on 235 paired days) | Insight card + “Show the facts” |
| **Prospective short-horizon** | “If I protect bedtime near 02:20 for the next 3 nights, what happens to debt and readiness?” | Sleep debt, recent response pattern | Sleep recovery plan |
| **Training posture** | “If I take the easy session today vs rest, how does that affect tomorrow’s recovery band given current HRV?” | Recovery inputs, load, historical response | Daily guidance alternatives |
| **Consistency** | “What if wake-time variance stayed under 45 min for two weeks?” | Existing wake-time analysis | Schedule coaching |
| **Load management** | “What if weekly load stays at current low level while sleep improves?” | Load trend + sleep | Training narrative |

Start simple and local. You do not need a 100k-person world model on day one. The personal correlations and baselines already present in the dashboard are enough for useful first-order counterfactuals.

### 19.3 Design and safety constraints for counterfactuals

1. **Ground in the user’s own history.** Prefer “on nights like this for *you*” over population averages.
2. **Bound by historical peaks and feasibility.** Do not suggest sleep durations or training loads the user has never approached.
3. **Separate observation, projection, and suggestion.** The user must be able to reject the suggestion without rejecting the data.
4. **Never use clinical or diagnostic language.** Frame as “projected readiness / energy pattern,” not disease risk.
5. **Show uncertainty.** “Based on 235 paired days, an extra hour has historically been associated with ~6 readiness points for you — individual nights vary.”
6. **Keep “Show the facts.”** The underlying pairs, windows, and coefficients remain inspectable.
7. **Tone:** autonomy-supportive, never fear- or guilt-based. Research coaching prompts explicitly ban alarmism and jargon such as “counterfactual” or “simulation” in user-facing copy; present as natural “if you continue current routine vs if you adjust X.”

### 19.4 Concrete product features

**Near-term (local, using existing data):**

- Sleep debt recovery plan with projected effect on the next 2–3 nights’ likelihood of clearing target, derived from the user’s own short-sleep → readiness history.
- Daily guidance that includes a light alternative projection: “If you take the easy session, recovery signals are expected to stay in band; if you push harder while sleep debt remains elevated, historical pattern suggests a higher chance of a softer day tomorrow.”
- Insight cards that answer one clear “what if” using the already-computed personal correlations.

**Medium-term:**

- Simple interactive counterfactual: user adjusts a bedtime or session intensity slider; the product updates a projected readiness / energy band using the personal response model.
- Weekly plan that contrasts “current trajectory” vs “one adjusted lever” (sleep timing, easy volume, or consistency).

**Longer-term (if data volume and modeling mature):**

- Multi-week trajectory projections conditioned on habit changes, similar in spirit to the research world-model + coaching agent systems, still running locally or with explicit user consent for any heavier compute.

### 19.5 How nudges and counterfactuals reinforce each other

- A counterfactual supplies the *reason* and the *expected magnitude* of change.
- A well-designed nudge supplies the *small, concrete next action* and the *choice architecture* that makes the action easy.
- Together they move the product from “here is your data” to “here is what is likely if you continue, here is what is likely if you adjust this one lever, and here is the smallest useful step.”

This combination — transparent personal counterfactuals + autonomy-preserving, context-aware nudges — is still rare among commercial apps and is a realistic path to best-in-class coaching quality while preserving the honesty that is already a core strength of this dashboard.

## 21. Additional Lenses Previously Under-Weighted

The earlier sections covered competitive positioning, human testing, AI language, feedback loops, architecture, researched UX, analytics, nudging, and counterfactuals. Several important lenses were only touched lightly or not at all. They connect directly to what is already recommended.

### 21.1 Onboarding, cold-start, and time-to-first-value

Health and fitness apps lose most users in the first days. Research consistently shows that day-1 retention is weak unless the product delivers a *personal* insight quickly. Strategies that work: import existing history, compute something personal immediately, and show one specific insight about *this* user before asking for more commitment.

**Connection to this product:**  
You already have the opposite of a cold-start problem for the primary user — rich Garmin history is present. The risk is the inverse: a *hot-start overwhelm* problem. The first open of a dense Scientist-style view can feel like the cold-start failure mode in reverse.

**Implication:**  
Coach mode is not only a daily UX choice; it is the correct first-run and returning-user default. First value should be the status sentence + primary recommendation within seconds. Progressive disclosure (already recommended) and the dual-mode shell are the practical solution to both cold-start and hot-start failure modes.

### 21.2 Uncertainty, missingness, and data quality communication

Dashboards that treat every number as equally certain create false confidence or, when users notice gaps, distrust. Best practice is to surface coverage, confidence, and missingness at the decision point — not only behind a details panel.

**Connection to this product:**  
You already do better than most commercial apps: sparse running is acknowledged, nights without usable sleep are excluded from averages, and baseline coverage (28 / 90 / full archive) is shown. This is a strength to systematize.

**Implication:**  
- Make data-quality / coverage a first-class visual language (e.g., muted styling or explicit “limited data” labels when windows are thin).  
- Attach confidence language to AI guidance (“signals agree” vs “mixed / sparse”).  
- Never invent confidence when recent running is sparse or sleep records are incomplete — the current honest empty states are the correct pattern to extend.

This reinforces the “Show the facts” and multi-signal reasoning recommendations.

### 21.3 Digital health anxiety and emotional design

Wearable data can increase awareness or increase anxiety. Alarmist language, red flags for normal variation, and comparison to idealized ranges are known contributors to digital health anxiety. Care-over-scare design uses neutral, contextual, supportive tone and normalizes day-to-day noise.

**Connection to this product:**  
The resting-pulse card is medically responsible but still leans clinical. Sleep shortfall framing is accurate but demotivating. AI summaries that restate numbers without context can feel like a report card.

**Implication:**  
- Lead with human interpretation and personal range before the raw number or the medical caveat.  
- Prefer “your body is coping; another short night will likely show up” over pure deficit language.  
- Keep urgent medical disclaimers, but demote them so they do not dominate the emotional first read.  
- This is the same principle already stated under progressive disclosure, nudging ethics, and counterfactual tone constraints.

### 21.4 Voice, tone, and content design system

A coherent voice turns a collection of cards into a single coach. Without it, AI summaries, findings, and metric labels drift into different registers (clinical, cheerleader, data-dump).

**Recommended voice attributes (aligned with existing strengths):**  
- Supportive realist (neither cheerleader nor doctor)  
- Specific and concrete  
- Transparent about uncertainty and sources  
- Autonomy-preserving  
- Calm under variation  

Codify this in a short voice & tone guide and apply it to every AI template, finding, and empty state. This is the content counterpart to the Coach vs Scientist dual mode.

### 21.5 Edge cases and life context

Real users get sick, travel across time zones, deload, take injury time, or have cycle-related variation. A product that only models “normal training weeks” will give brittle advice.

**Connection:**  
Sparse running is already handled honestly. Extend the same honesty to explicit edge states: “recent data looks like travel or illness — guidance is more conservative” or “load is intentionally low; this is a good window to protect sleep.” Subjective “I feel…” chips are the fastest way to capture these states before full context models exist.

### 21.6 Accessibility beyond baseline

Keyboard chart interaction and ARIA are already present and good. Next layer:

- Consistent focus order when many `<details>` expand  
- Reduced-motion preference  
- High-contrast / color-independent encoding of recovery vs caution (not color alone)  
- Screen-reader friendly “Show the facts” and confidence language  
- Touch targets and readout persistence on mobile (already partially noted)

### 21.7 Evaluation: how you know you are best-in-class

Define product success metrics that match the ambition:

| Goal | Example signals |
|------|-----------------|
| Daily decision quality | % of opens that produce a clear primary action; time-to-decision |
| Trust | Use of “Show the facts”; low rate of dismissed insights that later prove correct |
| Habit support | Sleep consistency improvement; subjective feel correlation with objective recovery |
| Calm | Reduced bounce from Today; qualitative “I don’t feel judged” feedback |
| Depth without overwhelm | Scientist mode usage among power users; retention of casual users on Coach mode |
| Safety | Zero diagnostic overclaim incidents; correct handling of sparse / anomalous data |

These metrics should guide the roadmap order below.

### 21.8 Human coach / clinician handoff

A clean, user-controlled week story or summary export (already on the longer-term list) serves both self-reflection and optional sharing with a coach or clinician. Keep it optional, privacy-preserving, and generated from the same transparent facts the user already sees. This extends the “honesty” advantage into the human relationship layer that pure apps lack.

### 21.9 Attention economy and notification ethics

Because the product is local-first and insight-rich, the temptation will be to notify often. Resist. Prefer:

- Pull (user opens and gets value) over push  
- Context-aware soft cues only when recovery state or sleep debt makes them relevant  
- Weekly story as the main reflective cadence  

This aligns with adaptive nudging research and with the goal of reducing digital health anxiety.

---

## 22. Consolidated & Reprioritized Roadmap

The following order optimizes for: (1) immediate daily decision quality and calm, (2) trust and intelligence quality, (3) architecture that unlocks depth without density, (4) advanced coaching (counterfactuals, trajectories), (5) polish and ecosystem.

### Phase 0 — Foundation for calm daily use (do first)

1. **Coach / Scientist dual-mode shell** with Coach as default (solves hot-start overwhelm and progressive disclosure in one move).  
2. **Today hero rewrite**: status sentence + decisive primary recommendation + clear alternative + elevated “why / signals used.”  
3. **Subjective “I feel…” chips** (even if re-weighting is light at first).  
4. **Voice & tone pass** on all AI summaries and findings: stop pure restatement; adopt observation → personal baseline → implication → action.  
5. **Sleep debt reframed** as a 2–3 night recovery plan with autonomy-preserving language.

*Why first:* These changes improve the half-awake morning experience immediately and do not require a full data-layer rewrite.

### Phase 1 — Intelligence quality & trust

6. **Multi-signal insight templates** + confidence / mixed-signal language.  
7. **Surface existing personal correlations** (sleep ↔ readiness, etc.) as living rules of thumb.  
8. **Light personal-history counterfactuals** in guidance and sleep plan (“if bedtime moves earlier…”).  
9. **Data-quality / coverage language** systematized across cards and charts.  
10. **Emotional design pass** on resting pulse, shortfall, and anomaly copy (care-over-scare).

*Why next:* Turns the already-strong data into coaching that feels personal and safe.

### Phase 2 — Architecture that enables depth without density

11. **Local data store + view layer** (replace monolithic 5 MB snapshot for ongoing use).  
12. **Lazy history**: calendar / timeline navigator; day and run detail on demand.  
13. **Simple / Detailed chart modes** + comparison presets; persistent mobile readout.  
14. **Breadcrumbs / context bar** for orientation.  
15. **Body Battery / energy curve** used for light time-of-day cues.

*Why here:* Unlocks scale and performance while protecting the calm Coach experience.

### Phase 3 — Advanced coaching & learning loops

16. **Interactive short-horizon counterfactuals** (bedtime / load slider → projected band).  
17. **Accept / dismiss / complete logging** to improve future ranking of recommendations.  
18. **Quiet intrinsic progress acknowledgment** (consistency, recovery rebound) without streak guilt.  
19. **Weekly story** with one focus lever.  
20. **Edge-state handling** (illness, travel, deload) via subjective input + conservative guidance.

### Phase 4 — Ecosystem & polish

21. **User-controlled week / clinician summary export**.  
22. **Accessibility hardening** (reduced motion, focus order, non-color encoding).  
23. **Richer multi-week trajectories** if/when personal models are stable.  
24. **Optional multi-source ingest** (still local-first, explicit consent).  
25. **Notification ethics policy**: minimal, context-aware, mostly pull.

## 24. Final Synthesis

You already possess the rare combination of deep personal data, source transparency, local AI with visible facts, and honest handling of sparse data. Most competitors choose either opacity + strong prescription or openness + weak synthesis.

The remaining work, ordered above, is to:

1. Make the daily experience calm and decisive (Coach mode + better guidance + subjective input).  
2. Make the intelligence multi-signal, personal, and uncertainty-aware.  
3. Rebuild the delivery architecture so depth never costs calm.  
4. Add counterfactuals and gentle, autonomy-preserving nudges so the product coaches forward, not only reports backward.  
5. Protect emotional safety, accessibility, and attention at every step.

Executed in that order, the product can be simultaneously more honest than Garmin Connect, more transparent than Whoop, more actionable than Oura on training decisions, and more coherent than Apple Health — while remaining a tool the user still feels in control of.

## 25. Product Manager Perspective

### 25.1 Jobs-to-be-done (the real product)

Users do not open this dashboard to “see numbers.” The core jobs are:

| Job | When | Success looks like |
|-----|------|--------------------|
| **Decide today’s training posture** | Morning, half-awake | Clear default action + safe alternative in <10 seconds |
| **Understand why the body feels this way** | After a bad night or flat session | Multi-signal story grounded in *my* history |
| **Protect long-term consistency** | Weekly / when motivation dips | One focus lever, not a list of failures |
| **Stay in control of the narrative** | Always | “Show the facts” still works; no black-box score |
| **Optionally brief a human coach** | Occasional | Clean, honest week story |

Everything on the roadmap should map to one of these jobs. Features that do not should be deprioritized.

### 25.2 Positioning & differentiation (PM statement)

**For** serious recreational athletes and self-coached runners who already wear a Garmin (or similar)  
**Who** want decisive daily guidance without giving up transparency or control  
**The product** is a local-first recovery & training decision companion  
**That** turns dense wearable history into calm, inspectable, multi-signal recommendations  
**Unlike** Garmin Connect (data-rich but weak synthesis), Whoop (strong prescription, opaque), Oura (recovery-strong, training-weak), or Apple Health (passive aggregator)  
**It** keeps the user in the loop with personal baselines, counterfactuals, and “show the facts.”

This positioning should govern copy, feature prioritization, and what *not* to build (social leaderboards, financial incentives, opaque composite scores that cannot be inspected).

### 25.3 North-star and supporting metrics

**North-star (proposed):**  
*Percentage of morning opens that result in a clear, user-accepted primary action within the session*  
(i.e., the product successfully closed the “what should I do today?” job).

**Leading indicators:**
- Time from open → primary recommendation visible
- Rate of subjective-feel input
- Use of “Show the facts” / expand details
- Coach vs Scientist mode distribution
- Dismissal / completion rate of the primary recommendation
- Sleep-consistency or recovery-rebound improvements over rolling windows

**Guardrail metrics (do not harm):**
- Digital health anxiety signals (qualitative + any spike in “alarm” language engagement)
- Sparse-data honesty (no fabricated confidence)
- Notification opt-out / ignore rate

### 25.4 Product principles (PM operating system)

1. **Decision over dashboard.** If a screen does not help a decision, demote or hide it behind Scientist mode.
2. **Personal baseline over population.** Every comparison defaults to *you*.
3. **Transparency is a feature.** “Show the facts” is non-negotiable; it is the moat.
4. **Autonomy over compliance.** Always offer a credible alternative path.
5. **Calm is a performance feature.** Anxiety-inducing design reduces long-term adherence.
6. **Local-first, inspectable AI.** Intelligence that cannot explain itself is not shipped as guidance.

### 25.5 What a PM should protect against

- Feature creep into “another metrics grid”
- Opaque scores that win short-term engagement but destroy trust
- Gamification that rewards volume over recovery
- Notification systems that train users to ignore the product
- Building for the power-user Scientist at the expense of the daily Coach job

---

## 26. Product Designer Perspective

### 26.1 Core design problem

The product currently solves for *completeness*. The design problem to solve next is **selective attention under low cognitive bandwidth** (the morning open). Everything else (depth, charts, history) must remain available without competing for that first 10 seconds.

### 26.2 Information architecture recommendations

- **Two modes, one product:** Coach (default) and Scientist (explicit). Already recommended; design must make the switch reversible, visible, and non-punitive.
- **Today as a decision surface**, not a summary of all domains. Sleep / Training / Trends become supporting stages.
- **Progressive disclosure as the primary pattern:** status → recommendation → signals used → full facts → deep history.
- **Consistent object model:** every metric card should answer the same questions in the same order (what is it, vs my baseline, what does it imply, what can I do).

### 26.3 Interaction & visual system

- **Hierarchy scale:** one primary action, one secondary alternative, everything else quiet.
- **State design:** empty, sparse, loading, anomaly, and “signals disagree” are first-class designed states, not afterthoughts.
- **Chart interaction:** Simple vs Detailed; persistent mobile readout; keyboard parity already present — protect it.
- **Micro-copy as UI:** the status sentence and the “why” line *are* the interface for most users.
- **Motion:** purposeful, reduced-motion respectful; energy/Body Battery curves can move gently; numbers should not flicker.
- **Color:** semantic and color-blind safe; recovery / caution / neutral never rely on hue alone.

### 26.4 Design process suggestions

- Prototype the **morning decision path** first (paper → high-fidelity → instrumented). Measure time-to-decision and clarity of next action.
- Test with **half-awake / low-attention** scenarios, not only desk reviews.
- Maintain a living **voice & tone** and **component** library so AI-generated copy and new cards stay coherent.
- Treat “Show the facts” expand states as designed experiences with hierarchy, not raw data dumps.

### 26.5 Designer–PM shared artifacts worth creating

- Job stories for the five jobs above
- Decision-flow diagrams for Today (happy path + sparse data + mixed signals + user overrides)
- Content design guidelines (voice, counterfactual language, uncertainty phrasing)
- Accessibility acceptance criteria for every new chart or expand panel

---

## 27. How Else AI Can Be Used — Analytics, Insights & Presentation

Beyond the insight engine, multi-signal reasoning, and counterfactuals already described:

### 27.1 Narrative & storytelling layer

- **Daily story (1–3 sentences):** synthesizes the highest-signal facts into a readable paragraph the user could say out loud.
- **Weekly chapter:** longer narrative with one theme, what improved, what to protect next week.
- **Trajectory stories:** “If the last 14 days continue…” vs “If the sleep plan sticks…”
- Keep every narrative expandable to the underlying facts (same trust model).

### 27.2 Adaptive presentation / generative layout

Research on adaptive health dashboards shows LLMs can reorganize widgets from behavioral signals (dwell, reorder, explicit feedback). Practical, lower-risk version for this product:

- Learn which cards the user expands or acts on.
- In Coach mode, quietly promote high-utility cards and demote ignored ones.
- Never hide core safety / recovery signals.
- Always allow reset to default layout.

### 27.3 Anomaly explanation & “why unusual”

When a metric is outside personal range, AI should answer *why it might be* using correlated local signals (late bedtime, high load yesterday, travel, illness chip) rather than only flagging the anomaly. This turns red flags into understandable stories.

### 27.4 Insight ranking & personalization of *what* is shown

Not every computed insight deserves the same surface area. Rank by:
- Actionability today
- Strength of personal evidence
- Novelty (not the same insight three days running)
- User feedback (dismissed insights drop in rank)

### 27.5 Multi-modal presentation

- **Voice summary** (already hinted by narration meta): optional spoken morning briefing.
- **Glanceable complication / widget** for watch or phone: status + primary action only.
- **Exportable brief** for human coach (Phase 4).

### 27.6 Simulation & planning (extends counterfactuals)

- “Plan my next 7 days” given a goal (e.g., protect recovery while keeping some quality).
- Constraint-aware: respects current debt, recent load, and user-stated constraints (“knee is noisy”).
- Output is a short plan + the projected effect language, still inspectable.

### 27.7 Continuous learning from local feedback

Accept / dismiss / complete / “I did the alternative” become training signal for which recommendations and which insight templates are useful *for this user*. No cloud required; local preference model.

### 27.8 Guardrails for all AI presentation

- No diagnostic language
- Uncertainty always visible when confidence is low
- Source facts always one expand away
- User can reject the narrative without rejecting the data

---

## 28. Responsible Gamification — What Fits This Product

Gamification works for engagement; it can also increase stress, guilt, and volume-chasing. Evidence and ethics point to a narrow, recovery-aligned design.

### 28.1 What to avoid

- Streaks that break on rest days or illness
- Leaderboards or social pressure (unless explicitly opt-in and private cohorts)
- Points for more volume regardless of recovery
- Loss-framed guilt (“you lost your streak”)
- Competition that ignores readiness

### 28.2 What can work here (aligned with recovery & autonomy)

| Mechanic | How to implement | Why it fits |
|----------|------------------|-------------|
| **Recovery as the “win”** | Celebrate rebound days, sleep consistency, and “you protected recovery” | Matches Whoop-style insight that rest is performance; flips volume culture |
| **Readiness-aware quests** | Low readiness → mobility / easy / technique “quest” that still gives a sense of progress | Turns rest into an active choice, not a failure |
| **Grace & week-based consistency** | Soft consistency markers with grace for life events | Avoids streak anxiety |
| **XP / acknowledgment for process, not only outcome** | Credit for following the plan, logging feel, or completing the sleep plan — not only for hitting a score | Supports autonomy and process focus |
| **Self-exploration over competition** | Personal history records, “new personal insight unlocked,” trajectory improvements | Evidence shows self-exploration gamification produces less stress than competition |
| **Visible progress on the jobs** | “Decision clarity streak” (you opened and left with a plan) is healthier than “training volume streak” | Aligns with north-star |

### 28.3 Design rules for any game layer

1. Recovery and consistency are first-class scored / celebrated behaviours.
2. Grace days and life-context overrides are built in.
3. Opt-in; never required for core value.
4. No public ranking by default.
5. Language stays supportive-realist (same voice system).
6. User can hide the game layer entirely.

Used this way, light gamification supports the PM jobs (especially consistency and daily decision) without fighting the emotional-design and anxiety constraints.
